title: Hedyotis biflora: How to Spot and Control It in Your Palay
metaTitle: Hedyotis biflora in Rice: Identification and Control
metaDescription: Hedyotis biflora, known as pisak or dalumbang, is a slender broadleaf weed of lowland rice. Learn to spot it and stop it before it drops seed.
excerpt: Hedyotis biflora is a small, slender broadleaf weed. Farmers know it as pisak, dalumbang or palarapdap. It grows in irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. This page shows you how to spot it among your palay and how it takes from your crop. It also shows how to control it before it sets seed.

heroImage.alt: Hedyotis biflora with slender branched stems and small oval leaves growing between rice hills

blocks.text:
Hedyotis biflora is a small annual herb from the coffee family, Rubiaceae. Its stems are thin and branched, and the plant either stands upright or spreads out low. Farmers in different places call it dalumbang, kaddok na kalinga, palarapdap, pisak or pisek. Because it stays small and slender, it is easy to miss between the rice hills.

You will find this damo in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields. Its life lasts one season. Within one crop it sprouts, flowers, sets seed and dies. Seed is its only way to spread. The tiny seeds fall around the mother plant and wait in the soil for the next crop. So a patch you ignore this season can come back thicker next time.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Hedyotis biflora
rows: Dalumbang, kaddok na kalinga, palarapdap, pisak, pisek
Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Look low between the rice hills for a small herb with thin, branching stems. Some plants stand upright, while others sprawl. The leaves are oval to oblong, set in pairs, and sit on very short stalks. Like other broadleaf weeds, the leaves are wide with netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. When it blooms, its tiny flowers come in small umbrella like clusters of 2 to 8. A similar weed, Hedyotis corymbosa, also grows in rice, but its leaves are much narrower and taper to a point.

items: A small herb with thin, branched stems, standing upright or spreading low between rice hills.
Oval to oblong leaves on very short stalks, set in pairs along the stem.
Thin stems that branch many times, giving the plant a light, airy look.
Tiny flowers grouped in small umbrella like clusters of 2 to 8.
Look alike tip: Hedyotis corymbosa shares its local names but has long, narrow leaves.

blocks.text:
This weed is small, but it still competes with your palay. It takes water, nutrients and fertilizer from the same soil your rice roots use. When many plants come up together, they fill the open spaces between young rice hills. Young rice feels this the most, because it is still building roots and tillers.

Since it is an annual that spreads by seed, every plant that flowers adds to the seed supply in your bukid. That is why it returns season after season. Its seeds can also end up mixed with the harvested palay. Thick weedy patches can give insects a place to hide near the crop as well.

items: Weed early and often. Small, slender plants are easy to miss, so walk the paddy carefully while the rice is still young.
Pull it before the tiny flower clusters form seed. Once seeds drop, they wait in the soil for the next crop.
Keep good water in the paddy where you can. Small seeded annual weeds sprout more easily on moist, exposed soil than under standing water.
Clean the bunds and field edges as well, since plants there can seed back into the paddy.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Hedyotis biflora down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Hedyotis biflora Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Hedyotis biflora?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Hedyotis biflora

items.q: What is Hedyotis biflora called in local languages?
items.a: Farmers use several names for it, depending on the place. You may hear dalumbang, kaddok na kalinga, palarapdap, pisak or pisek. The same names also cover its close cousin, Hedyotis corymbosa. To tell them apart, look at the leaves. This one has oval to oblong leaves, while its cousin has long, narrow ones.

items.q: How do I control pisak in my rice field?
items.a: Prevention comes first. Prepare the land well, use clean binhi, and keep good water in the paddy. Hand weed while the plants are small, and remove them before they flower. If the stand is heavy, pick a herbicide for broadleaf weeds that matches the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Is such a small weed really worth pulling?
items.a: Yes. One plant does little harm. The trouble starts when many plants sprout together from the seed in your soil, because together they take water and fertilizer from your palay. Each plant you leave also drops more seed for next season. So pulling early keeps the problem small and cheap to manage.
